NEW YORK CITY DEPARTMENT OF  
HEALTH AND MENTAL HYGIENE 
Michelle Morse, MD, MPH 
Acting Health Commissioner 
 
 
 
September 3, 2025 
 
 
U.S. Department of Veterans Affairs 
Via electronic submission - Federal Register: Reproductive 
Health Services 
Re: The Department of Veterans Affairs (VA) proposing to 
reinstate the full exclusion on abortions and abortion 
counseling from the medical benefits package. 
Abortion is necessary, life-changing medical care. Abortion 
bans prevent many people from accessing care they want and 
need, causing preventable harm and death. The NYC Health 
Department strongly opposes the Department of Veterans 
Affairs moving forward with this proposed rule and removing 
these necessary health services. 
New York State has the fifth largest veteran population in the 
United 
States.1 
Over 
200,000 
veterans 
and 
active 
servicemembers, as well as their families and caretakers, 
currently live in New York City – making it an epicenter for 
those who have proudly served and continue to serve our 
country.2 While the majority of veterans in New York City 
identify as male, about 10% identify as female and this 
population is steadily rising. 3 Family members and dependents 
eligible for VA medical benefits will also be impacted by 
exclusions on abortion care .  
The proposal does not provide a reasoned explanation for 
eliminating the existing rule regarding reproductive healthcare. 
Diminishing reproductive healthcare for veterans and 
CHAMPVA beneficiaries does not serve public health and 
denies veterans autonomy over their own bodies. Many people 
will be forced to travel long distances to obtain needed abortion

care, seek other methods of abortion beyond their method of choice, or continue a pregnancy against their 
will with potentially harmful health-related or financial consequences.4 People who do not obtain an 
abortion when they want one are four times more likely to live in poverty afterwards and experience long-
lasting effects on their educational attainment and job opportunities.5 
This proposal will shift the logistical and financial burdens of abortion care from a federal agency with 
responsibility for providing care for veterans to state and local governments and nongovernmental health 
care providers, and onto veterans themselves to come up with the out-of-pocket costs for their health care. 
Nearly 50% of veterans of childbearing age live in highly restrictive abortion access states. Rescinding the 
existing rule would leave veterans and their families in these states with no access to needed healthcare 
services or force them to travel to states or cities that provide abortion care, such as New York City, 
substantially increasing the populations served to include these VA/CHAMPVA residents in addition to 
their own. 
Abortion bans with limited exceptions, as exists in this proposal, rarely allow patients to receive the care 
they need.6 In this regard, the proposed language is vague and would create confusion and fear, preventing 
clinicians from practicing evidence-based medicine. This policy would cause unnecessary delays or denials 
of care, further endangering the health and life of patients forced to continue pregnancies. Moreover, the 
operative language of the proposal draws an arbitrary distinction between veterans and CHAMPVA 
beneficiaries. 
Ensuring safe, legal access to abortion care to people of all ages is a public health necessity. As evidence-
based healthcare comes under fire, the New York City Health Department continues to support access for 
our veterans and anyone else seeking care to low barrier, high quality sexual and reproductive healthcare in 
NYC. To this end, the VA should withdraw this rule proposal and maintain existing requirements regarding 
reproductive healthcare. 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
Sincerely,   
 
 
       
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
Michelle Morse, MD, MPH 
Acting Health Commissioner 
Chief Medical Officer 
NYC Department of Health and Mental 
Hygiene
